items.title: 11.4 Unreactive nature of alkanes towards polar reagents

source_refs.note: Topic 11.4, printed page 252. The Did You Know box on combustion is carried as a sentence.

blocks.text: The alkanes or paraffins (Latin parum = little, affinis = affinity) are inert towards acids, alkalis, oxidising and reducing agents under ordinary conditions. Their lack of reactivity is explained by the non-polarity of their bonds: the electronegativities of carbon (2.5) and hydrogen (2.1) do not differ appreciably, so the bonding electrons in C-H and C-C bonds are equally shared, making the bonds almost non-polar and generally unreactive. The unreactivity is also explained by the inertness of the sigma bond: its electrons are held very tightly between the nuclei, making it a very stable bond that needs a lot of energy to break. Hydrocarbon combustion produces CO2, a greenhouse gas; incomplete combustion releases carbon monoxide and particulate matter with serious health and environmental consequences.

blocks.caption: Why alkanes are unreactive
rows: C (2.5) and H (2.1) share the C-H and C-C electrons almost equally; polar reagents find no charged site
electrons held tightly between the nuclei; much energy needed to break them

blocks.prompt: Explain why alkanes have high stability and do not undergo addition reactions (Quick Check 11.3a; exercise Q.2c).
blocks.explanation: All their bonds are strong, non-polar sigma bonds with no electron-rich region to attract electrophiles and no polarity to attract nucleophiles, so acids, alkalis and redox reagents leave them alone at ordinary temperatures. Addition needs a multiple bond to open; alkanes are saturated, so they can only react by substitution or by thermal breakdown.

items: Paraffins ('little affinity'): inert to acids, alkalis, oxidisers and reducers because C-H and C-C bonds are non-polar (electronegativity 2.5 vs 2.1) and sigma bonds are strong.
